title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about starting well at university: what it really means to excel, and the mindset and motivation that successful students bring from the start. By the end you will be able to explain what excelling means, describe how a growth mindset and self-efficacy support success, and tell learning motivation apart from performance motivation.

These are not abstract ideas. How you think about your own ability, and what drives you to study, shape the effort you put in and how you respond when work gets hard. Getting this right at the start changes how the rest of your degree feels.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what it means to excel at university
describe how a growth mindset and self-efficacy support success
distinguish learning motivation from performance motivation in your own studying.

title: In real academic practice
body: Starting well is the foundation the rest of your degree is built on. The mindset you bring to your first assignments, the belief that you can improve with effort, and the reasons you study all shape how you work in every module that follows. Build these now and they carry through your studies, and into the working life your degree leads to.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what it means to excel: success as more than marks. Second, a growth mindset: how believing you can improve, and trusting you can succeed, support your studies. Third, understanding your motivation: the difference between studying to perform and studying to learn. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can explain what it means to excel at university.

title: Orientation
body: When people talk about doing well at university, they often mean one thing: high marks. Marks matter, but they are not the whole story, and chasing them alone is not what excelling means. Excelling is about how you approach your studies, not just the grades you come away with. This lesson looks at what excelling really is, so you can aim for it from the start.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are just starting out, and you may never have thought about success as anything other than a grade. That is normal. At this stage you are not expected to have it all worked out. The aim is to understand what excelling means and to recognise the mindset behind it, so you have something clear to aim for.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: define excelling at university as more than achieving high marks
describe success as both academic performance and personal development
recognise excelling as a mindset you bring to {{context}}, not a fixed trait.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Excelling at university is not the same as getting top marks. Marks measure one kind of success, academic performance, but success has a second side too: personal development, the way you grow as a thinker and a person through your studies. A student who earns a good grade and also becomes more confident, curious and independent has excelled more fully than one who earns the grade alone.

Excelling is best understood as a mindset rather than a fixed trait. It is not something you either have or lack; it is an approach you choose and build. This lesson is about what that approach is; the lessons that follow are about the mindset and motivation that drive it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a time you did well at something. Was it only the result that made it feel like success, or also what you learned or how you grew along the way?

title: Summary
body: Excelling at university means more than high marks. Success has two sides: academic performance, the grades and skills, and personal development, the way you grow as a thinker and a person. Excelling is a mindset you bring, not a fixed trait you are born with. You can now define excelling in this fuller way and recognise the mindset behind it. The next lesson looks at the growth mindset and self-belief that make excelling possible.

_items.title: See pages 9 to 16 of Chapter 2, 'Excelling at university: Mindset, motivation, and goals', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that excelling is a mindset. This lesson looks closely at the mindset that sits behind success: a growth mindset, and the self-belief that comes with it. The difference between students who keep improving and students who stall is often not ability, but how they think about ability itself.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to have a perfect growth mindset already; almost no one does. The aim here is to notice the difference between a growth and a fixed mindset, and to understand self-efficacy, so you can spot these in yourself and begin to choose the more helpful response.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: tell a growth mindset apart from a fixed mindset
explain what self-efficacy is and why it matters for studying
identify a growth-mindset response to a setback in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A fixed mindset treats ability as set: you are either good at something or you are not, and effort will not change much. A growth mindset treats ability as something that develops: with effort, good strategies and feedback, you can get better. The same difficult result means different things to each. To a fixed mindset it says you have reached your limit; to a growth mindset it says you have more to learn.

Self-efficacy is a close partner of the growth mindset. It is your belief that you can succeed at a particular task. Strong self-efficacy does not mean thinking everything is easy; it means trusting that, with effort, you can cope and improve. That belief shapes whether you take on a challenge or avoid it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of something you once believed you were just not good at. What would it look like to treat that ability as something you could build, rather than something fixed?

title: Summary
body: A growth mindset treats ability as something you can build with effort, strategies and feedback, where a fixed mindset treats it as set. Self-efficacy, the belief that you can succeed at a task, is its close partner and shapes whether you take a challenge on. You can now tell the two mindsets apart and identify a growth-mindset response to a setback. The next lesson turns to what drives your effort: your motivation.

_items.title: See pages 16 to 21 of Chapter 2, 'Excelling at university: Mindset, motivation, and goals', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You have seen that excelling is a mindset, and that a growth mindset and self-belief support it. This lesson is about what drives you: your motivation. Two students can work equally hard for very different reasons, and the reason matters. It shapes what you do when no one is watching and when the work stops being easy.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to have one pure kind of motivation; most people have a mix. The aim is to tell the two main kinds apart and to notice which one is driving you, so you can lean towards the kind that supports deeper learning.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish learning (mastery) motivation from performance motivation
recognise what each kind of motivation looks like in how a student studies
give an example of learning-focused motivation in your own study of {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Performance motivation is the drive to do well in front of others: to get the grade, to prove you are able, to avoid looking as though you are struggling. Learning motivation, sometimes called mastery motivation, is the drive to understand and get better at something for its own sake. Both can lead to hard work, but they pull in different directions when work gets difficult.

The difference shows under pressure. A student driven mainly by performance may avoid a hard topic in case they look weak at it. A student driven by learning is more likely to take the hard topic on, because the point is to understand, and a struggle is part of that. Noticing which drive is stronger in you is the first step to steering it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a subject you are studying. When you work at it, are you more driven to do well in front of others, or to understand it for its own sake? What tells you which?

title: Summary
body: Performance motivation is the drive to perform well in front of others; learning (mastery) motivation is the drive to understand for its own sake. Both fuel effort, but they part ways under pressure: learning motivation is more likely to take a hard topic on. You can now tell the two apart and recognise them in how a student studies. With a clear sense of what excelling is, the mindset behind it and the motivation that drives it, you have the foundations to start well.

_items.title: See pages 21 to 23 of Chapter 2, 'Excelling at university: Mindset, motivation, and goals', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Excelling is no longer just about marks: it is something you can describe and begin to aim for. You can explain what excelling means, success as both academic performance and personal development, approached as a mindset rather than a fixed trait. You can describe how a growth mindset and self-efficacy support success. And you can tell learning motivation apart from performance motivation. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, starting well is something you practise in every module. Each assignment you approach as a chance to grow and not only to score, each setback you meet with effort rather than retreat, each time you study to understand rather than only to perform, is this mindset at work. It is also what working life rewards: people who keep learning, believe they can improve, and know what drives them go further.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced Starting, Progressing and Succeeding courses take these foundations into setting and regulating your own goals, and into building the graduate capital that employers value. Going wider: the same foundations underpin Reflective Practice, Academic Writing and Researching, where you put the mindset to work on real tasks.

title: Explore the concept
definition: Doing more than passing: growing as a thinker and a person, not only earning high marks.
extendedDefinition: At university, excelling means treating success as both academic performance and personal development, and approaching your studies as a mindset you build rather than a fixed talent you either have or lack.
example: A student who earns a good grade and also becomes more curious, confident and independent has excelled more fully than one who earns the grade alone.
instruction: Select the button to reveal the meaning, then read on.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students on the same first-year module.

{{learner-a}} has one aim: the highest mark possible. {{learner-a}} learns what the marker wants, revises exactly that, and is pleased with a strong grade. The mark is real, but nothing else has changed. {{learner-a}} is no more curious, confident or independent than before, and has little interest in the subject beyond the assessment. This is success measured only as academic performance.

{{learner-b}} wants to do well too, but also wants to understand the subject and become a better thinker. {{learner-b}} reads around the topic, takes on ideas that are not strictly needed for the mark, and finishes the module more confident and more interested than before. The grade is good, and {{learner-b}} has grown as well. This is excelling: academic performance and personal development together.

Both students passed well. Only {{learner-b}} treated the module as a chance to grow, not just a grade to earn.

title: Aiming to excel
body: These habits turn the idea into something you do. Try them in your own studies.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I thought about what I want to learn from this module, not just the mark I want?
Am I letting myself be curious about the subject beyond the assessment?
Am I noticing how I am growing as a thinker, not only what grades I earn?
Do I treat my ability to do well as something I can build, rather than fixed?
Would I still count this as success if the grade were only average but I had learned a lot?
Am I approaching my studies as an opportunity, not just a hurdle to clear?

_items.feedback: Yes. Excelling joins academic performance with personal development.

_items.text: Achieving the highest possible marks, whatever else happens.
_items.feedback: Marks are one kind of success, but excelling is more than the grade.

_items.feedback: Excelling is a mindset you build, not a fixed talent.

_items.feedback: Meeting the brief earns marks, but it is not the fuller success excelling describes.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that goes beyond the grade to how you grow.
_incorrect.final: Excelling joins good marks with personal development. The other options stop at the grade, at fixed talent, or at the bare brief.

title: Formative check: recognising excelling
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's approach closer to excelling?

ariaQuestion: What made the second student's approach closer to excelling?

_items.text: They earned a good grade and also grew more confident and interested in the subject.
_items.feedback: Yes. Growing as well as scoring is excelling.

_items.text: They earned a higher grade than the first student.
_items.feedback: The point was not a higher grade; both passed well.

_items.text: They spent far longer on the module than the first student.
_items.feedback: Time spent was not the difference; growing as well as scoring was.

_items.text: They focused only on what the marker wanted.
_items.feedback: That describes the first student, who chased the mark alone.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student scored well and grew as a thinker, which is excelling.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student gained beyond the grade.
_incorrect.final: The second student excelled because they grew in confidence and interest as well as scoring well, not because of a higher grade or more time.

title: Formative check: excelling as a mindset
displayTitle: You are beginning a module in {{context}}. Which approach shows excelling as a mindset rather than chasing marks alone?

_items.feedback: Yes. That approach treats {{context}} as a chance to grow, which is excelling.

_items.text: Working out the minimum needed for a good grade and doing only that.
_items.feedback: That treats the module as a hurdle, not a chance to grow.

_items.text: Assuming you will either be good at {{context}} or not, and leaving it there.
_items.feedback: That is a fixed-trait view; excelling is a mindset you build.

_items.text: Avoiding anything not directly tested in the assessment.
_items.feedback: Curiosity beyond the assessment is part of excelling.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, excelling means aiming to understand and grow, not only to score.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that aims to grow and understand, not only to pass.
_incorrect.final: Excelling as a mindset in {{context}} means aiming to understand and grow as well as to score. The other options chase the mark or treat ability as fixed.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four everyday moments where a fixed mindset says one thing. Turn each card to see how a growth mindset reads the same moment.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: A fixed mindset hears a hard task as proof of a limit. A growth mindset hears it as a sign there is more to learn. The task has not changed; what you tell yourself about it has.
To a fixed mindset a low mark is a verdict on your ability. To a growth mindset it is feedback on this attempt: information about what to try differently next time.
A fixed mindset sees needing to work hard as a sign you lack talent. A growth mindset sees effort as how ability is built, the way practice builds a skill in sport or music.

Self-efficacy is believing you can succeed at a task with effort. It is not blind confidence. It is what lets you take a challenge on rather than avoid it, and it grows each time you cope with something hard.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students each get a disappointing mark on their first essay.

{{learner-a}} reads the grade and reaches the obvious conclusion: I am not cut out for this subject. The low mark feels like a verdict on fixed ability, so {{learner-a}} quietly avoids the next challenging task and stops asking for help, in case it confirms the worst. This is a fixed mindset, and the low self-efficacy that comes with it.

{{learner-b}} is just as disappointed, but reads the mark differently: this attempt did not work, so what can I change? {{learner-b}} studies the feedback, asks the tutor what a stronger essay would do, and treats the next task as a chance to improve. The belief that effort will pay off, rather than being wasted, is self-efficacy at work. This is a growth mindset.

Both students met a setback. Only {{learner-b}} read it as information to act on rather than a limit to accept.

title: Building a growth mindset
body: These habits turn the idea into something you do. Try them in your own studies.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: When something is hard, do I tell myself I can get better at it with effort?
Do I treat a low mark as feedback on this attempt, rather than a verdict on my ability?
Do I look at what to change next time, instead of giving up on the task?
Do I ask for help when I am stuck, rather than hiding the difficulty?
Do I remind myself that effort is how ability is built, not a sign I lack talent?
Can I recall a time I improved at something through practice, as evidence I can do it again?

title: Formative check: growth versus fixed mindset
displayTitle: Which of these is a growth-mindset response rather than a fixed-mindset one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a growth-mindset response?

_items.text: Treating a hard task as a sign there is more to learn, and something effort can improve.
_items.feedback: Yes. A growth mindset sees ability as something that develops.

_items.text: Taking a hard task as proof you have reached the limit of your ability.
_items.feedback: That is the fixed-mindset reading.

_items.text: Avoiding difficult work so you do not risk looking less able.
_items.feedback: Avoiding challenge is a fixed-mindset move.

_items.text: Assuming people are simply born good or bad at a subject.
_items.feedback: A growth mindset sees ability as something that develops.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading difficulty as a chance to learn, improvable with effort, is the growth mindset.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that treats ability as something effort can build.
_incorrect.final: The growth-mindset response treats a hard task as more to learn. Seeing it as a fixed limit, avoiding it, or assuming people are born able are all fixed-mindset moves.

title: Formative check: self-efficacy
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student's reaction to the low mark show about self-efficacy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student's reaction show about self-efficacy?

_items.text: They believed effort would pay off, so they acted on the feedback to improve.
_items.feedback: Yes. Trusting that effort will pay off is self-efficacy.

_items.text: They were sure the subject was simply too hard for them.
_items.feedback: That reflects low self-efficacy and a fixed mindset.

_items.text: They decided the mark proved they lacked the ability.
_items.feedback: Reading a mark as a verdict on fixed ability is the opposite of self-efficacy.

_items.text: They avoided the next task in case it went badly.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the challenge is low self-efficacy, which the first student showed.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Believing effort would pay off, and acting on it, is self-efficacy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Self-efficacy is the belief that you can succeed with effort. Which option shows that?
_incorrect.final: The second student showed self-efficacy by trusting that effort would pay off and acting on the feedback. The other options show low self-efficacy.

title: Formative check: a growth-mindset response
displayTitle: You get a low mark on an early piece of work in {{context}}. Which is the growth-mindset response?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the growth-mindset response to a low early mark?

_items.text: Look at the feedback, ask what a stronger piece would do, and treat the next task as a chance to improve.
_items.feedback: Yes. Acting on feedback to improve is the growth-mindset response in {{context}}.

_items.text: Conclude you are not cut out for {{context}} and ease off.
_items.feedback: That reads one mark as a fixed verdict.

_items.text: Avoid the next challenging task in case it confirms the mark.
_items.feedback: Avoiding challenge is a fixed-mindset, low-self-efficacy move.

_items.text: Decide the subject is simply too hard and stop asking for help.
_items.feedback: Withdrawing effort and help is the fixed-mindset response.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the growth-mindset response acts on feedback to improve next time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that treats the mark as feedback to act on, not a verdict.
_incorrect.final: The growth-mindset response in {{context}} uses the feedback to improve. Giving up, avoiding the next task, or withdrawing help are fixed-mindset responses.

title: Explore the concept
body: Two kinds of motivation, and what tells them apart. Step through each tab.
instruction: Select each tab to read about it.

_items.title: Performance motivation
_items.body: Performance motivation is the drive to do well in front of others: to earn the grade, to prove you are able, to avoid looking as though you are struggling. It can push you to work hard, especially when the work is visible and marked.

_items.title: Learning (mastery) motivation
_items.body: Learning motivation, or mastery motivation, is the drive to understand and get better at something for its own sake. The reward is the understanding itself, not only the mark. It keeps you going even when no one is watching.

_items.title: What happens under pressure
_items.body: The two part ways when work gets hard. Performance motivation can lead you to avoid a difficult topic in case you look weak at it. Learning motivation is more likely to take the hard topic on, because a struggle is part of understanding.

_items.title: Which is driving you?
_items.body: Most people have a mix of both, and performance motivation is not wrong. But leaning towards learning motivation tends to support deeper understanding and keeps you studying when the pressure is off. Noticing which is stronger is the first step to steering it.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students may each choose a topic for the same open essay.

{{learner-a}} picks the safest, most familiar topic, the one most likely to earn a high mark with least risk. The hard, interesting question is left alone in case it goes wrong. The essay is competent and the mark is fine, but {{learner-a}} has learned little that is new. This is performance motivation: the drive is the grade and how it looks.

{{learner-b}} is drawn to the harder question because it is the one worth understanding, even though it carries more risk. {{learner-b}} struggles with it, learns a great deal in the process, and comes away understanding something genuinely new. The mark matters, but it is not the main point. This is learning, or mastery, motivation.

Both students wrote a good essay. Only {{learner-b}} chose the task for what could be learned from it.

title: Studying to learn
body: These habits turn the idea into something you do. Try them in your own studies.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: When I study, can I name something I want to understand, not just a mark I want?
Do I sometimes choose the harder, more interesting task over the safest one?
Do I keep working at a topic even when no one is checking?
When work gets difficult, do I stay with it rather than switch to something easier?
Am I studying this because I want to understand it, or only to look good?
Can I point to something I learned recently that I did not strictly need for a mark?

title: Formative check: two kinds of motivation

_items.text: Studying to understand a subject and get better at it for its own sake.
_items.feedback: Yes. Understanding for its own sake is learning motivation.

_items.text: Studying mainly to earn the grade and prove you are able.
_items.feedback: That describes performance motivation.

_items.text: Choosing the safest task so you are sure to look good.
_items.feedback: Playing safe to look good is performance motivation.

_items.text: Avoiding hard topics in case you seem to struggle.
_items.feedback: Avoiding difficulty to protect how you look is performance motivation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Learning motivation is the drive to understand and improve for its own sake.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about understanding for its own sake, not the grade or how you look.
_incorrect.final: Learning motivation studies to understand for its own sake. The other options are driven by the grade or by how you look, which is performance motivation.

_items.text: They chose the harder question because it was worth understanding, even though it carried more risk.

_items.feedback: That is the first student, driven by performance.

_items.feedback: Caring only about the grade is performance motivation.

_items.text: They picked the most familiar topic to avoid any risk.
_items.feedback: Avoiding risk to protect the mark is performance motivation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Taking on the harder question to understand it is learning motivation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the choice made for understanding rather than for the safe mark.
_incorrect.final: The second student showed learning motivation by taking on a harder question to understand it. The other options protect the mark or image, which is performance motivation.

title: Formative check: learning motivation in practice

_items.text: Take the tricky topic on because understanding it is worth the effort, even if it is harder.
_items.feedback: Yes. Choosing to understand, despite the difficulty, is learning motivation in {{context}}.

_items.feedback: Playing safe for the mark is performance motivation.

_items.feedback: Studying for how it looks is performance motivation.

_items.text: Avoid the topic because it might expose a weakness.
_items.feedback: Avoiding difficulty to protect your image is performance motivation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, taking the topic on to understand it is learning motivation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the choice made to understand, not to protect the mark or your image.
_incorrect.final: Learning motivation in {{context}} takes the tricky topic on to understand it. The other options protect the mark or how you look, which is performance motivation.

_items.text: Measuring your worth only by the grade you receive.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Treating ability as something you can build is the excelling mindset.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that treats ability as something effort can build.

body: A student gets a poor mark and decides the subject is simply too hard for them, then avoids the next challenge. This reaction best reflects...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student decides a subject is too hard and avoids the next challenge. This reflects...

_items.text: a fixed mindset and low self-efficacy.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading a mark as a fixed limit and withdrawing is a fixed mindset with low self-efficacy.

_items.text: a growth mindset.
_items.feedback: A growth mindset would treat the mark as feedback to act on.

_items.text: strong self-efficacy.
_items.feedback: Strong self-efficacy would mean trusting effort could improve things.

_items.text: learning motivation.
_items.feedback: This is about mindset and self-belief, not what drives the student.

_feedback.correct: That's right. This is a fixed mindset with low self-efficacy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the student read their ability and their belief they could improve.

body: What is self-efficacy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is self-efficacy?

_items.text: Your belief that, with effort, you can succeed at a particular task.
_items.feedback: Yes. Self-efficacy is the belief that effort can bring success.

_items.text: A natural talent you are born with.
_items.feedback: Self-efficacy is a belief, not an inborn talent.

_items.text: The certainty that everything will be easy.
_items.feedback: It is not blind confidence that things are easy.

_items.text: The grade you expect to receive.
_items.feedback: It is a belief about your capacity, not a predicted grade.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Self-efficacy is believing you can succeed with effort.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Self-efficacy is a belief about what you can do with effort.

body: A student takes on a harder topic because understanding it is worth the effort, even at the risk of a lower mark. Which motivation is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student takes on a harder topic to understand it despite the risk. Which motivation?

_items.text: Learning (mastery) motivation.
_items.feedback: Yes. Choosing to understand for its own sake is learning motivation.

_items.text: Performance motivation.
_items.feedback: Performance motivation would protect the mark and avoid the risk.

_items.text: No motivation.
_items.feedback: The student is clearly motivated, towards understanding.

_items.text: A fixed mindset.
_items.feedback: This is about what drives the student, not how they view ability.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Studying to understand, despite the risk, is learning motivation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which motivation is driven by understanding rather than the mark?

body: Which of these is a sign of performance motivation rather than learning motivation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a sign of performance motivation?

_items.text: Choosing the safest task mainly to be sure of looking able.
_items.feedback: Yes. Playing safe to look able is performance motivation.

_items.text: Taking on a hard topic to understand it better.
_items.feedback: That is learning motivation.

_items.text: Studying a subject because you find it genuinely interesting.
_items.feedback: Interest for its own sake is learning motivation.

_items.text: Continuing to work at something when no one is checking.
_items.feedback: Working with no audience points to learning motivation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Playing safe to protect how you look is performance motivation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the choice driven by how you look rather than by understanding.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what it means to excel at university, a growth mindset and self-efficacy, and the difference between learning and performance motivation. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one approach you can bring to your studies.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to have it all working together smoothly. The aim is to see these three ideas as one approach rather than three separate topics, so it carries on past this course and into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how what excelling means, a growth mindset and self-efficacy, and learning motivation connect as one approach to studying
show this joined-up approach at work in a worked example of a student studying
plan one way you will bring this approach to your study of {{context}} from the start

title: Concept: definition
body: This approach is the three ideas working as one. You treat each piece of work as a chance to grow, not just a grade to earn. You meet it with the belief that effort will pay off. And you study to understand, not only to perform. Excelling, a growth mindset and learning motivation are not separate lessons; they are three parts of one way of studying.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this approach shows up in how you meet each piece of work, not in a one-off decision. You treat a task as a chance to grow, trust that effort and good strategies will help, and study to understand rather than only to score. Brought to every module, the three ideas become one steady way of working.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a subject you are studying. How could you bring these three together in it: treating work as a chance to grow, trusting you can improve, and studying to understand? What is one thing you would do differently from next week?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: These three ideas are strongest when you use them together. You treat work as a chance to grow, meet it believing effort pays off, and study to understand, again and again across your modules. It is this joined-up approach, not any single idea, that helps you start well and keep improving.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The practice as one cycle
body: Excelling is these three ideas working as one continuing practice, not three separate lessons. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Take it on
_items.body: Treat each piece of work as a chance to grow, not just a mark to earn.

_items.title: Believe
_items.body: Meet the task believing that effort and good strategies will pay off.

_items.title: Understand
_items.body: Study to understand the subject, not only to perform in the assessment.

_items.title: Carry forward
_items.body: Look back on what you learned, and carry it into your next piece of work. The cycle keeps turning.

title: Worked example
body: Two students begin the same module. One aims only at the mark, picks safe topics, and treats ability as fixed, so a hard task feels like a threat. The other treats the module as a chance to grow, trusts that effort will pay off, and chooses the topic worth understanding. Over the term the second student learns more and grows more, because the three ideas worked together as one approach.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to bring it all together
body: Use these to keep the three ideas working as one approach, rather than as separate lessons.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Am I treating this piece of work as a chance to grow, not just a grade to earn?
Do I believe I can improve at this with effort and better strategies?
Am I studying to understand the subject, not only to look good?
When work gets hard, do I stay with it rather than retreat?
Am I bringing this same approach to each new task, not starting from scratch?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat excelling, a growth mindset and learning motivation as one approach rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat excelling, a growth mindset and learning motivation as one approach rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat excelling, a growth mindset and learning motivation as one approach rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because they support each other: aiming to grow, believing you can improve, and studying to understand all pull in the same direction.
_items.feedback: Yes. Together they make one way of studying, each strengthening the others.

_items.text: Because once you know all three, you never need to think about how you study again.
_items.feedback: The approach helps because you keep using it, not because it is a one-off.

_items.text: Because it means you can ignore your marks completely.
_items.feedback: Marks still matter. The approach is about more than marks, not instead of them.

_items.text: Because three separate ideas are always harder to remember than one.
_items.feedback: It is not about memory. The three work together because they support one another.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Excelling, a growth mindset and learning motivation work together as one approach to studying.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the three ideas strengthen each other when you use them together.

displayTitle: A student takes on a harder module topic to understand it better, believes they can improve with effort, and treats the work as a chance to grow rather than only a grade. What does this show?
body: A student takes on a harder module topic to understand it better, believes they can improve with effort, and treats the work as a chance to grow rather than only a grade. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student takes on a harder module topic to understand it better, believes they can improve with effort, and treats the work as a chance to grow rather than only a grade. What does this show?

_items.text: The three ideas working as one approach: learning motivation, self-belief and excelling together.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three are at work in how this student approaches the task.

_items.text: Performance motivation on its own.
_items.feedback: Choosing the harder topic to understand it is learning motivation, not performance motivation.

_items.text: A fixed mindset about ability.
_items.feedback: Believing they can improve with effort is a growth mindset, not a fixed one.

_items.text: Chasing marks and nothing more.
_items.feedback: The student treats the work as a chance to grow, which is more than chasing marks.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Learning motivation, a growth mindset and excelling are all at work here, as one approach.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where all three ideas are working together.

displayTitle: What does it mean to bring excelling, a growth mindset and learning motivation together as one approach to studying?
